motley

/MOT-lee/ — emphasis on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is motley is made up of many different and mismatched kinds of people or things gathered together.

A motley collection of mismatched chairs filled the community hall.

Worked Example

The community theater's cast was motley: a retired banker played the villain, two high school students were the lovers, a nurse delivered comic relief, and a schoolteacher gave the soliloquies.

The cast members come from completely different professions and backgrounds—they don't match or coordinate in any obvious way. 'Diverse' would work, but motley more precisely captures the sense of mismatched people gathered together, emphasizing their incongruous origins.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assorted: Assorted means of various different sorts mixed together — assorted candies, assorted sizes — and it stays cheerfully neutral. Motley is pointed: a motley group is not just varied but visibly mismatched, its pieces clashing as though nobody ever meant them to share a room.

miscellaneous: Miscellaneous means made up of unrelated odds and ends — the label on the drawer where leftovers go. It says the items do not belong to one category. Motley goes further: the mismatches are visible and clashing, a jumble you notice at a glance.

hodgepodge: A hodgepodge is a noun naming the disorderly jumble itself — 'the essay was a hodgepodge of ideas.' Motley is the adjective that describes such a group: made of visibly mismatched, clashing kinds, gathered together without any coordination.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

uniform: all alike, with no variation

matching: deliberately alike in style or appearance

Where it sits · how clashing and thrown-together it is — uniform → matching → varied → motley

uniform vs. motley: Uniform is the opposite end of the scale from motley: a uniform set is identical throughout, while a motley one is a clashing jumble of mismatched pieces.

matching vs. motley: Matching sits near the opposite end of the scale from motley; matching things are chosen to go together, while motley things visibly do not match at all.

varied vs. motley: Varied is weaker than motley: a varied group has pleasant differences, while a motley one is so mismatched and thrown-together that it looks almost chaotic.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — motley

Root — motley: parti-colored, made of mixed colors (Anglo-Norman)

Put it together

Put it together: Motley entered English as a single word for cloth woven of clashing colors — the patchwork suits worn by court jesters. From mixed-color cloth it broadened to describe any mismatched assortment of people or things.

Use the root in a new word: mottled

Use the root in a new word: mottled: The pony's mottled coat was blotched with patches of gray, brown, and white — mottled grew out of motley and keeps its sense of mixed, uneven color.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Motley is the word when you want to emphasize that a collection is made up of different and visibly mismatched elements. Use it for groups or objects that don't coordinate well but are gathered or assembled together. If things are intentionally mixed from different sources (like an artistic collection), eclectic is more precise.
